lessons.title: What Can You Afford? Renting vs. Owning Costs
objectives: Total the costs of renting over time with rent increases.
List the monthly costs of owning beyond the mortgage.
lessons.hook: Two fictional listings: $1,950/month apartment vs. $340,000 townhouse. Which costs more per month? Vote.

notes.body: Lenders often use 28% (housing) and 36% (all debt) of gross income; your budget may require less.
Rent, renters insurance, utilities, deposit; rent can rise at renewal.
P&I, taxes, insurance, PMI, HOA, maintenance, utilities.

examples.problem: Gross $90,000; car payment $420. Max housing payment?

discussion: What non-financial factors affect renting vs. owning?
misconceptions: List all ownership costs on the board.
reflection: What would you look for in your first apartment lease?
lessons.extension: Compare two real listings in your area (public sites).

extend: Find the income needed for a given home price.

lessons.realWorld: Many landlords require gross income of about 3× the monthly rent.

lessons.title: Modeling a Mortgage
objectives: Analyze the first payments in an amortization schedule.
lessons.hook: “How much of your first $2,200 mortgage payment goes toward owning the house?” Predict.

notes.body: Same installment formula as auto loans with n = 180 or 360.
First payments are mostly interest; equity from paydown builds slowly at first.
A 1-point rate change can shift payments by hundreds of dollars.

discussion: Why might someone choose a 30-year loan even if they can afford a 15-year payment?
misconceptions: Half the payments = half the loan paid.
reflection: How does a mortgage rate change affect a buyer?
lessons.extension: Graph remaining balance vs. year for 15- and 30-year loans.

extend: Compute the effect of one extra payment per year.

lessons.realWorld: Mortgage rates change daily and depend on credit, down payment, and loan type.

lessons.title: The Full Cost of Owning a Home
objectives: Compute PITI including PMI and HOA.
lessons.hook: Show a fictional Loan Estimate; students circle every number that is not P&I.

notes.body: Taxes and insurance often add 20–35% to P&I; PMI applies below 20% down.
Down payment + closing costs (2–5%) + moving + reserves.

discussion: Why might a buyer put down less than 20%?
reflection: How much would you want saved before buying a home?
lessons.extension: Research the typical property tax rate in your town.

extend: Find when PMI can be removed (80% loan-to-value).

lessons.realWorld: Lenders must give a Loan Estimate within three business days of an application.

lessons.title: Rent or Buy? Equity and Opportunity Cost
objectives: Compute equity from appreciation and paydown.
Calculate the opportunity cost of a down payment.
Compare the net cost of renting and buying over a horizon.
lessons.hook: Claim: “Renting is throwing money away.” Debate briefly, then use the Decision Lab “Rent or Buy a Home?”.

notes.body: All outflows − equity at sale + opportunity cost of cash.
Buying usually needs several years to overcome transaction costs.
Appreciation, rent growth, rates, and horizon drive the answer.

examples.problem: $60,000 down payment invested at 5% for 7 years.

discussion: Under what assumptions does renting win? Buying?
misconceptions: Subtract interest, taxes, and fees that are gone.
reflection: Would you rent or buy at 25? At 35? Why?
lessons.extension: Run the Decision Lab with pessimistic and optimistic markets and write a memo.

extend: Model a home price decline scenario.

lessons.realWorld: Online rent-vs-buy calculators use the same structure with more detail (e.g., taxes).

solutionSteps: Owner outflows = $193,145.19; equity at sale = $99,279.96; opportunity cost = $14,138.96.
